identity_evidence.quote: A 63‐year‐old man presented with epigastric pain.

attribution_limitations: The text says the endoscopy five years earlier revealed multiple erosions and ulcers (Figure 1), and the Figure 1 caption describes the initial presentation with erosions, shallow ulcers and a white mucosal change around the ulcer. They are treated as the same endoscopy because the text cites Figure 1 for it.

The bypass is dated two weeks after diagnosis. The Figure 2 caption places the endoscopic and angiographic CT findings at diagnosis, so the endoscopy and CT are ordered before the bypass through that shared anchor; the source does not name a separate diagnosis event or its exact day.

The discussion says that once the stomach was fully dilated no white mucosal development was observed; it does not say whether this refers to the endoscopy at diagnosis or the postoperative endoscopy, so it is not recorded as a fact.

The discussion lists possible causes (complete SMA occlusion, celiac artery stenosis, stretching of the gastric wall by insufflation) of the mucosal color change; these are hypotheses and not asserted causes.
The aortic CT was performed on the same day as the endoscopy and the caption places both at diagnosis, so they are recorded as same_time; which was done first within that day is not stated.

claims.text: A 63-year-old man with hypertension and hyperlipidemia, and no diabetes or chronic kidney disease, was referred to the authors' hospital for epigastric pain and recurrent gastric ulcers of undetermined cause. Five years earlier an upper endoscopy for persistent severe epigastric pain showed multiple erosions and ulcers; biopsy showed only inflammatory findings, he was Helicobacter pylori antibody negative and used no NSAIDs or anti-thrombotics, and the mucosa improved with proton pump inhibitors.
